source.title: Taming Polysemanticity in LLMs: Provable Feature Recovery via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Si-Yu Chen; Heejune Sheen; Xu-Yuan Xiong; Tianhao Wang; Zhuo-Ran Yang

record.tranche_reason: The paper takes sparse mixtures of monosemantic features as its framework and develops SAEs for feature recovery. Its own results concern SAE recovery and consistency, not how often trained networks have polysemantic neurons or whether their mixed responses are caused by capacity pressure.
record.gate_note: The paper motivates its method with polysemantic representations and models them as sparse mixtures. It does not measure polysemantic-neuron prevalence or test whether individual neurons in trained LLMs respond to unrelated inputs. Its synthetic feature-recovery-rate (FRR) and real-data SAE comparisons are related feature-recovery results, not direct tests of the listed versions; cited observations about SAEs and TopK sensitivity are not this study's results. Synthetic FRR findings are recorded as none-version results below.
record.test_reason: The paper takes superposition-driven polysemanticity as its motivation and models activations as sparse nonnegative mixtures of monosemantic features. Its results all concern its own SAE training algorithms (BA/GBA): synthetic feature recovery, recovery theorems, and the reconstruction–sparsity frontier and seed consistency on Qwen2.5-1.5B MLP outputs. It never measures how often or why neurons of a trained network are polysemantic. The synthetic 'superposition regime' (n > d) is a constructed data model, not a test of whether trained networks pack features into neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that bias adaptation provably recovers all monosemantic features under their sparse-mixture model with Gaussian features. On Qwen2.5-1.5B MLP outputs, GBA matches the TopK (post-activation) sparsity-loss frontier, beats L1 and BA, and is nearly tuning-free. GBA is more consistent across seeds than TopK. Add the caveat that L1 was more consistent than GBA in three of four consistency settings.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates sparse-autoencoder bias adaptation and feature recovery, rather than the original neuron-visualization or SoLU measurement procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Synthetic SAE recovery varies with co-occurrence, target activation frequency, dimension, feature occurrence, and feature cutoff. In real-data SAE comparisons, reconstruction and sparsity tradeoffs vary with activation choice and GBA grouping settings; these are not polysemanticity measurements.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic sparse-mixture data, GBA and TopK SAEs recover nearly all planted features (FRR near 1), with GBA using few active neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs trained with bias adaptation recover planted monosemantic directions from superposed synthetic data.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic SAE recovery depends on co-occurrence (sharp drop near ρ2 ≈ 1/√n), target activation frequency relative to n and d, and feature occurrence and strength.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature recoverability depends on data co-occurrence and on feature frequency and strength.

record.problems: Synthetic findings use a constructed sparse-mixture model and do not establish the prevalence or causes of polysemantic neurons in trained networks. The paper says its theoretical dynamics assume Gaussian-distributed features, and that verifying incoherence in real-world data is challenging. Real-data feature consistency is a proxy because ground-truth features are unavailable. Many plotted results are described qualitatively rather than with tabulated numeric values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No direct polysemanticity results were reported. Real-data SAE reconstruction/sparsity comparisons and cross-run consistency results were left out because they evaluate SAE performance or consistency, not the listed claim versions. The paper's theorem and other synthetic FRR experiments beyond the selected conditions were not entered as additional rows because they likewise measure feature recovery rather than polysemanticity.

untested.parts: All: no share or layerwise rate of polysemantic MLP neurons in LLMs. The Qwen SAEs report only reconstruction, sparsity and consistency.
All: superposition is assumed as framing and built into synthetic data, not tested as the cause of neuron polysemanticity in trained networks.
All: the JumpReLU vs ReLU comparison concerns SAE activations and the sparsity-loss frontier, not polysemantic neuron share in the model.

record.verdict_notes: A method paper. The polysemanticity and superposition language is motivation only. No version of the claim is tested, so no verdicts are given. All rows are the study's own method performance and could reasonably be dropped as claim rows.

versions.untested_parts: Vision-model neurons and responses to unrelated image inputs.
Share and layerwise distribution of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer language models.
Whether capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity in trained networks; the paper assumes a sparse-mixture framework and tests SAE feature recovery within it.
Polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Changes in the share of polysemantic neurons by activation, architecture, or regularization, and the performance cost of reducing that share.
Whether canonical mixed-response neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs, and how often truly unrelated mixtures occur.
Sensitivity of polysemanticity judgments to activation range or explanation scoring.
